quiz.title: Unit 8 SAQ 01
quiz.headline: Kennedy, the new states, and the arms race
quiz.prompt: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question.
quiz.instructions: Answer all three parts. For each part, Answer the question directly, Prove it with specific historical evidence, and Explain how the evidence supports your answer. On the AP exam each part earns one point. This is self-assessment practice, not official College Board scoring.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice in AP short-answer format. Model answers show one strong response; other accurate, well-supported answers can earn the point.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: John F. Kennedy, president of the United States, inaugural address, January 20, 1961
stimulusBlocks.citation: John F. Kennedy, Inaugural Address, January 20, 1961. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (inaugural/1961-Kennedy.txt).
stimulusBlocks.note: “New States” are countries that had recently won independence from colonial rule; seventeen African colonies became independent in 1960 alone. “The deadly atom” refers to nuclear weapons.
stimulusBlocks.text:
Let every nation know, whether it wishes us well or ill, that we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe, in order to assure the survival and the success of liberty. . . .

To those new States whom we welcome to the ranks of the free, we pledge our word that one form of colonial control shall not have passed away merely to be replaced by a far more iron tyranny. We shall not always expect to find them supporting our view. . . .

But neither can two great and powerful groups of nations take comfort from our present course -- both sides overburdened by the cost of modern weapons, both rightly alarmed by the steady spread of the deadly atom, yet both racing to alter that uncertain balance of terror that stays the hand of mankind's final war.

scaffold.label: Answer
scaffold.text: Respond directly to the task verb: identify, describe, or explain.

scaffold.label: Prove
scaffold.text: Name a specific person, place, institution, or development.

scaffold.label: Explain
scaffold.text: Show how or why the evidence answers the question.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE pledge Kennedy makes to newly independent states.
criteria: States a specific pledge from the passage.
Connects it to the new states Kennedy addresses.

model.answer: Kennedy pledges that the end of colonial rule will not be followed by a harsher form of domination.
model.prove: He promises the “new States” that “one form of colonial control shall not have passed away merely to be replaced by a far more iron tyranny.”
model.explain: By “iron tyranny” he means Soviet-backed communism, so the pledge offers US support against communist takeovers in former colonies.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also identify his statement that the United States will not always expect the new states to support its views.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way the United States or the Soviet Union competed for influence in newly independent states in the period 1950 to 1990.
criteria: Names a specific method and place.
Explains how the method was meant to win influence.

model.answer: The superpowers backed opposing sides in proxy wars fought in newly independent states.
model.prove: In Angola after independence in 1975, the Soviet Union and thousands of Cuban troops supported the government, while the United States and South Africa backed rebel forces.
model.explain: By arming local allies, each superpower tried to bring a new state into its bloc without fighting the other directly.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain economic aid, such as Soviet help building Egypt's Aswan High Dam or the US Alliance for Progress in Latin America, or covert action such as the US-backed coup in Guatemala in 1954.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way the historical situation in which Kennedy spoke shaped his message in the passage.
criteria: Describes a specific feature of the situation in early 1961.
Explains how it shaped what Kennedy says.

model.answer: Kennedy spoke as decolonization was creating many new states that both superpowers hoped to win as allies.
model.prove: Seventeen African colonies became independent in 1960, and Castro's Cuba had recently turned to the Soviet Union for support.
model.explain: That situation explains why he reassures the new states and warns rivals, presenting the United States as the protector of their freedom rather than a new colonial power.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain how the growing nuclear arsenals of both superpowers shaped his warning about the “balance of terror,” or how an audience of allies and rivals shaped his firm tone.
